about.first_note: Pleadli Police and Pleadli DPP were built first because investigation, referral, perusal, and prosecution form a useful early end-to-end connection, not because Courts, Lawyers, and Prisons are later stages of the same product. They are separate applications, each built around its own requirements.
about.lead: Pleadli exists to provide the digital infrastructure that makes that possible: software built for each participant's own work, connected only where a legitimate relationship exists.
about.meta_description: Pleadli exists to provide the digital infrastructure that makes justice institutions work together without becoming the same institution: software built for each participant's own work, connected only where a legitimate relationship exists.

centralization.p1: Connecting institutions doesn't mean putting all their records into one shared database. A case gets a continuous identity that follows it across the whole process, but what stays separate is who owns the records: police records belong to police, prosecution decisions belong to the DPP, and so on.
centralization.title: Connection without centralization

fragmentation.p1: A single matter can pass through police, prosecution, courts, and prisons, and today each of those stages usually runs on its own paperwork, with almost nothing connecting them. The same facts get re-entered at every handoff, and nobody outside one institution can confirm where a case actually stands.
fragmentation.p2: Pleadli exists so institutions don't have to recreate the same context every time a matter crosses a boundary.
fragmentation.title: Justice without fragmentation

purpose.p1: Police software should feel like police software. DPP software should feel like prosecution software. Court software should feel like court software. A lawyer's software should feel like legal practice software. Prison software should feel like custody software.
purpose.p2: Pleadli Police, Pleadli DPP, Pleadli Courts, Pleadli Lawyers, and Pleadli Prisons are separate applications, each designed around the work its users actually do, not one dashboard reused everywhere.
purpose.title: Purpose-built software

thread.p1: Responsibility for a matter moves: from an investigating officer, to a prosecutor, to a court, sometimes to a lawyer representing one side. Pleadli lets the underlying matter keep continuity even as that responsibility, and the professionals involved, change.
thread.title: One continuous thread

uganda.p1: Pleadli is starting with Uganda, designed around the justice system as it actually operates here, not a generic template applied to any country.
uganda.title: Built from Uganda outward

identity.body: A case keeps the same identity from investigation through to custody.
identity.title: One case, one identity

owned.body: Each application's records stay with the institution that created them, always.
owned.title: Institution-owned records

about.sign_in_body: Institutional users sign in to Pleadli to manage their organization, structure, and staff.
about.what_p1: Pleadli is a family of five applications, one for each part of justice: Pleadli Police, Pleadli DPP, Pleadli Courts, Pleadli Lawyers and Pleadli Prisons. Each is made for the work of the people who use it, runs on the office's own computers, and is useful on its own.
about.what_p2: Pleadli Orchestra, at pleadli.com, is what lets them play together: it gives each institution its address and certificate, carries sealed papers between offices that have agreed to work together, lets anyone check that a paper is genuine, and keeps licences and updates in order. It never holds an institution's records.
about.where_p1: Pleadli starts in Uganda, built around its laws, forms and offices as they actually work, and grows across East Africa: Kenya, Tanzania, Rwanda, Burundi, DR Congo and South Sudan, each with its own laws, deadlines and papers, in English, Kiswahili and French.
about.why_p1: When a file waits for paperwork, a person waits in a cell. In Uganda close to half of everyone in prison is on remand, not convicted, and in 2018 one in three human rights complaints against the police was about detention beyond the 48 hours the Constitution allows. Much of that delay is paper moving slowly between offices that each keep their own records.
about.why_p2: Pleadli does not replace those offices or merge their records. It gives each one a better tool for its own work, and a safe way to hand a case on.

ai.lead: DPP and Lawyers have Assist today: it summarises, drafts, and reads scanned papers, using the AI provider and key the office or practice chooses. Courts has an honest transcription seam, and Police and Prisons have no AI yet. Wherever AI appears the rule is the same: AI assists, it never becomes the record by itself.
ai.planned: Planned for Police and Prisons: transcription, summaries, and correspondence help, behind the same rules.
ai.privilege: Where AI touches privileged material, most acutely in Pleadli Lawyers, it inherits the application's own access controls: Assist is off until an administrator turns it on, the key is never shown back, and the accounts role cannot use it.

rules.adopt: Nothing becomes the record without a person: a draft becomes a document only when someone makes it one, papers Assist has named stay marked unchecked until a person edits them, and Courts' database refuses a machine transcript that nobody has corrected.
rules.context: Scoped context: Assist sees the application's own record of the matter, never another institution's records.
rules.deadlines: The application counts the law: every deadline Assist mentions is the one the app counted from the rules, not one the model worked out.
rules.provider: Provider-agnostic: the office or practice chooses the AI provider and brings its own key. Nothing is hard-coded to one model.

generated.body: Produced by a model, not yet looked at by anyone.
generated.title: AI generated

official.title: Official record

reviewed.body: A person has read it and either corrected it or accepted it as-is.
reviewed.title: Human reviewed

ai.title: Assist where it is built, one rule everywhere

apps.first_body: Police and DPP sit next to each other in a case's early life, investigation and prosecution, which makes the shared-identity, institution-owned-records model testable end to end without needing every application built first. This was a practical starting point, not a sequence the other applications wait in line behind.
apps.lead: Pleadli Police, Pleadli DPP, Pleadli Courts, Pleadli Lawyers, and Pleadli Prisons are separate applications, each designed around the work its users actually do. They are connected by Pleadli Cloud and by the cases they legitimately share, not merged into one product.
apps.lead_after: for a deep page per application.
apps.title: A family of purpose-built applications
apps.useful_body: Each application provides value on its own. A police station can use Pleadli Police to manage its own work whether or not a given case has reached the DPP. An individual lawyer can use Pleadli Lawyers for their own practice with no court connection at all. Interoperability becomes valuable when a legitimate relationship exists, it isn't a requirement for an application to be useful.

documents.lead: A charge sheet, a signed sitting record, or a filed bail application isn't supporting material for a case, it usually is the thing that matters legally. Pleadli treats a document as a first-class object moving through a real pipeline, not a file bolted onto the bottom of a form.

missing.docx: DOCX import and round-trip editing that preserves page structure, headers, footers, and signatures. Word export exists; bringing a Word file back in does not.
missing.folders: A real folder or file-manager view, browsing documents the way a case actually organises them.
missing.shared: A shared document architecture across applications; each one currently has its own separate model.

documents.per_app_title: How far each application actually goes

folder.title: Folder

freeze.title: Freeze

version.title: Version

documents.title: Documents are the record, not an attachment
documents.works_body: DPP, Courts, and Lawyers issue documents with a real reference number and a cryptographic hash, and freeze them once issued, database-enforced, not just a UI rule. DPP and Lawyers also seal them with signature and stamp and a verification code and QR anyone can check, with PDF and Word export. The folder browser and DOCX import ahead are real work, but they build on a foundation that's already sound.

how.address_body: When an institution registers on Pleadli Orchestra it receives an address that never changes, and a certificate signed by Pleadli saying which keys belong to it. Two offices still choose, person to person, whether to work together.
how.address_title: Every institution has an address and a certificate
how.admin_body: Platform administration manages Pleadli itself, which institutions exist and what they're entitled to use. Institutional administration is scoped to one institution: managing that institution's own units and members does not grant any visibility into another institution's structure.
how.apps_body: A police station, a prosecutor's office, a court, a prison or a law firm runs its own Pleadli app on its own computers. Its records are encrypted there and stay there. It works with no internet at all.
how.apps_title: Each office keeps its own app and its own records
how.country_body: Records never leave the institution. Backups go to storage the institution owns, such as a government data centre. For public institutions the relay itself can run on a government server in the country.
how.lead: Five apps that each work alone, and one Orchestra that lets them work together without merging their records.

entitlement.body: Whether an institution is allowed to use a given Pleadli application at all.
entitlement.title: Entitlement

membership.body: Which user belongs to which unit, and their title there.
membership.title: Membership

organization.body: One row per institution. Flat: Police, DPP, and future institutions sit side by side.
organization.title: Organization

unit.body: Self-referencing hierarchy within one institution, headquarters down to a station or office.
unit.title: Organization unit

how.post_p1: When a station sends a file to the prosecutor, the app seals it so that only that prosecutor's office can open it, and signs it so the office knows it came from that station and was not changed.
how.post_p2: The sealed file goes to the prosecutor's mailbox on the Orchestra relay, like a locked letter at a post office. The relay holds it only until it is collected and cannot read it. The prosecutor's app collects it, opens it, and a person decides whether to accept it. The decision comes back the same way.
how.post_p3: Offices in the same building talk directly over their own network. Nothing needs a special address or an open port: every office reaches the relay the way it reaches any website.
how.post_title: Passing a case on: a post office, not a shared file
how.principle_p1: A case should have one continuous identity as it moves between institutions. What stays separate is who owns the records: police records belong to the Uganda Police Force, DPP decisions belong to the DPP. An institution can reference a case without gaining access to another institution's internal records. Referenceability is not the same as visibility.
how.principle_p2: Today the same matter can carry a station CRB number, a separate DPP file number, and a separate court cause number, with no shared thread between them. Closing that gap without collapsing institutional ownership is the actual engineering problem.
how.public_body: Anyone holding a Pleadli paper can check it is genuine with its code. A person given a case tracking code can see the stage a case has reached, never its contents. Nobody can search case files by name.
how.real_body: Case-level work lives inside each application. Underneath them, Pleadli Cloud holds the organizational layer: institutions, their internal structure, and who belongs where.
how.real_title: What's real today: the organizational model
how.size_body: The same organizational model is what lets a Pleadli application serve an individual user, a team, or a larger organization, an individual lawyer and a law firm both use Pleadli Lawyers through the same model, structured differently. The hierarchy shape is up to each organization, Pleadli doesn't assume every institution looks like a police force.
how.status_note: The apps and their records exist today, and Pleadli DPP can already receive sealed files. Sending them from Pleadli Police, the Orchestra relay, addresses, certificates, paper checking and case tracking are being built now; see the Roadmap.
how.title: How Pleadli works

index.lead: How to start with Pleadli, how its apps work together, and how it keeps records safe. Written for the people who will use it and the people who decide on it.
index.next_body: Five apps that work alone, and one Orchestra that lets them work together.
index.scope_body: All five applications have real code today, at different levels of maturity. Police, DPP, Lawyers, and Prisons have a first Windows release that updates itself; Courts is not released yet and is the least field-tested. None of them is field-validated yet.
index.title: Documentation
index.what_body: Pleadli is a family of purpose-built applications, Pleadli Police, Pleadli DPP, Pleadli Courts, Pleadli Lawyers, and Pleadli Prisons, each with its own login, workflows, and records. Pleadli Cloud is the platform underneath all of them: identity, organizations, access, and the shared case identity that connects legitimate relationships across applications.

security.lead: Justice-sector records carry real consequences: a leaked statement, an altered custody record, or an unverifiable court order isn't a data-quality problem, it's a rights problem. Where this model is built, it's built into the database and the vault, not added afterward as a permissions flag.
security.offline_body: Every Pleadli application is designed to be fully useful with no internet connection at all. Cloud services and cross-institution exchange supplement local work; they are never a requirement for a station, prosecutor, court, advocate, or facility to keep working.

open.codesign: The Windows installers are not yet code-signed. Updates are signed, so an installed copy accepts only Pleadli’s own.
open.exchange: Exchange between machines (Prisons’ pinned-TLS facility sync, a Lawyers firm on one office network, the Police↔DPP interchange) has been tested on one machine or in test runs, never yet between separately installed machines in the field.
open.police: Police's attachment vault is not yet sealed under its key, and it does not yet keep the hash-chained audit trail the other four have.
open.roles: Roles are uneven across the applications. Lawyers decides by role who may sign, file, or pay out; the others do not yet draw lines that fine within one office.

security.per_app_lead: DPP, Courts, Lawyers, and Prisons share the full model through the common node-core package. Police has the encrypted database and the same key management, but not yet the sealed vault or the audit chain.
security.per_app_title: Where this actually stands, per application

audit.body: Every sensitive action is appended to a log where each entry is chained to the one before it, so a gap or a rewrite is detectable.
audit.title: A hash-chained audit log

db.body: The local database itself is encrypted at rest, not just individual fields inside it.
db.title: SQLCipher, not plain SQLite

key.body: The key that unlocks a machine's database lives in that operating system's own keystore, not in a config file or the database itself.
key.title: An OS-keystore key

vault.body: Attachments and issued documents are content-addressed and sealed, not stored as loose files on disk.
vault.title: A sealed document vault

security.title: Security is architecture, not a checkbox

start.help: Stuck at any step? Write to pleadli@pleadli.com or call +256 772 591 289.
start.lead: From download to your first record, in the order an office does it.
start.s1: Police, DPP, Lawyers and Prisons are ready for Windows on the Downloads page. Courts follows.
start.s1_title: Download the app for your office
start.s2: Open the installer. Windows may say it protected your computer, because the installer is not yet signed with a certificate: choose More info, then Run anyway. Later updates install themselves after asking.
start.s3: The first launch asks your country, language, office name, how the app is protected, and the first people who will use it. It takes a few minutes and needs no internet.
start.s4: Enter your first record. Every record can be printed, saved as PDF or Word, and carries a code that shows it is genuine.
start.s5: A headquarters registers its institution and attaches its offices; an advocate or a firm registers its practice. Each receives its Orchestra address.
start.s6: After 30 days on a computer, a licence adds connections to other offices, backup to your own storage and updates. Without one, the app and every record keep working.
start.s7: A station and its prosecutor's office agree to work together, check each other's fingerprints once, and from then on send sealed files to each other.
start.s7_title: Connect with the offices you work with
start.title: Getting started

stand.rest: Not yet: published checksums, Linux and macOS installers, and a release of Pleadli Courts.
stand.updates: Built: automatic updates, signed. An installed copy accepts only an update signed with Pleadli’s key.

step.court: The cause list, the sitting and the ruling are kept as the court's own papers, ready to sign.
step.decide: Charge, more inquiries, or no case. The station hears back through Pleadli, not a trip to the office.
step.dpp: Statements and exhibits travel sealed and signed, so the prosecutor reads exactly what the station sent.
step.dpp_title: The file goes to the prosecutor
step.lawyers: The defence follows every date and filing from their own office, without chasing the registry.
step.police: The officer records it at the station. The 48-hour clock starts on screen, and the statements are taken as papers.
step.prisons: The prison counts every day on remand and every trip to court, so no one is forgotten inside.

trust.law: Designed with Uganda's Data Protection and Privacy Act, 2019 in mind from the start, not added afterwards.
trust.law_title: Built around the law on personal data
trust.locked: Records are encrypted on each office's computer. A stolen laptop gives nothing away.
trust.named: Who wrote, changed, printed or sent a record is kept with it, and cannot be quietly erased.

home.trust_lead: A wrong date or a lost statement can cost someone their liberty. Security is part of how Pleadli is built, not added later.

every.after: After the trial the app keeps working and every record stays open, with a notice until a licence is added.
every.licence: A licence adds the Orchestra: connections to other offices, daily backup to your own storage, and updates of laws, forms and documents.
every.trial: 30 days free on each computer, with every feature, no card and no account needed to start.

faq.after_a: The app keeps working and every record stays open. A notice reminds you that the trial has ended, and connections, backup and updates wait for a licence.
faq.locked_a: No. Justice records must always be reachable. A station that cannot open its cell register is a danger, so Pleadli never locks records for payment.
faq.locked_q: Can our records ever be locked?
faq.read_a: No. Records stay on your computers, and backups go to storage your institution owns, never to Pleadli. Both are encrypted with keys only your institution holds.
faq.reinstall_a: No. The trial belongs to the computer, so a reinstall continues the same 30 days.
faq.reinstall_q: Does reinstalling start a new trial?
faq.where_a: Where your institution chooses: a government data centre in your country, your own server, or a drive in the office. Pleadli only shows whether each backup worked.
